BOI.name: Boise
BOI.excerpt: Beginning Monday, the area will be dry with a warming trend through Thursday, although seasonable temperatures are anticipated throughout.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Continued dry with normal temperatures through Friday morning.
- Precipitation chances increasing across higher terrain on the Idaho side Friday, becoming widespread in in ID and OR Saturday afternoon through Sunday.
- Drying and warming Monday through Thursday, then turning cooler and wetter Thursday and beyond.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Upper low center off the WA coast will hold stationary through Saturday evening but the low will elongate southward down the coast during that time. Subtropical Pacific moisture off Baja California will enter the south end of the low beginning Saturday and be drawn northward through the Great Basin along and ahead of a developing eastward-moving surface cold front. The front will become a focus for moderate to heavy pcpn as it moves across our CWA Saturday night through Sunday. Eastern OR will become wet before sunset Saturday, but rain may hold off in western ID (including the BOI metro) until around 7 PM MDT Saturday evening, after which several hours of steady pcpn will fall. SPC has a slight chance of thunderstorms in south-central ID Saturday night, which we have also included in our forecast. Accumulating snow will stay above 6500 feet while the bulk of pcpn is falling.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: Showers will continue through Sunday, tapering off throughout the day as the system departs. Snow levels Sunday will have lowered to 5.5-7kft MSL (increasing from west to east). These snow levels are higher than previous model runs consistent with a faster system trend. Snowfall will likely be limited to the mountains Sunday through Monday morning. In areas below the snow level less than 0.1 inches of rain is forecast, with only a trace to 0.03 inches forecast in the lower valleys. Sunday afternoon and evening will feature gusty winds following the cold frontal passage, with west to northwest gusts of 20-40 mph in the Snake River Plain.

Beginning Monday, the area will be dry with a warming trend through Thursday, although seasonable temperatures are anticipated throughout. Fog and stratus is possible Monday and Tuesday mornings with the recent precipitation and at the beginning of the warming trend. While there will be multiple opportunities for weak shortwaves to pass over the area, moisture will be limited and the shortwaves will just result in periods of increased high clouds.

BOU.name: Boulder / Denver
BOU.excerpt: By Wed an upper level ridge will build over the area ahead of another possible system moving across on Thu. For now, Wed looks dry and warmer ahead of the next system.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Areas of dense fog across portions of the plains overnight through mid morning Friday. This fog will impact the morning commute from Denver north to the Wyoming border
- Mild and mostly dry through the work week.
- Unsettled weather returns late this weekend and early next week. Mountain snow is likely (>70% chance) above 8500ft during this time. High uncertainty remains for the foothills and plains.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: For late tonight thru Fri morning main concern is how widespread dense fog may become along portions of the I-25 Corridor from Denver north to the Wyoming border and points eastward. HRRR has been consistent in showing fog developing over ern Larimer and Weld county by midnight and then spreading it southward into nrn portions of the Denver area by 3 am or 4 am. This fog would then linger thru the mid morning hours on Fri before lifting. In addition, soundings show some potential for drizzle as well.

Meanwhile, for the rest of Fri, the flow aloft will be SW with only isold showers possible in the mtns and far nern plains in the aftn. As for highs, readings will be in the lower to mid 60's across the plains, however, lingering low clouds could keep temps in the 50's over the far nern plains.

For Sat, little change is expected as SW flow aloft remains over the area. There still appears to be a weak disturbance embedded in the flow which may bring a chc of showers to portions of the higher terrain with an isold shower threat across the plains. Temperatures will remain in the upper 50's to mid 60's over nern CO.

Looking ahead to Sun and Sun night, there continues to be some uncertainty as to how an upper level trough along the West Coast evolves. The ECMWF and GFS now have a disorganized elongated upper level trough moving into the nrn Rockies and Great Basin by Sun night. Ahead of this feature, there will be quite a bit of subtropical moisture affecting the higher terrain, especially by Sun night. As a result, should see an increasing chc of showers over the higher terrain with snow levels dropping below 10000 ft late Sun night. Across the plains, it looks dry and windy thru Sun aftn as sfc low pres intensifies from ern WY into ern CO. By Sun night, latest data shows varying precip chances across the plains. For now, have kept in a chc of showers as a band of mid level QG ascent moves across overnight.

On Mon, the ECMWF and GFS have two main areas of energy associated with the elongated upper level trough. One piece stays over the nrn Rockies while a 2nd piece of energy moves across srn CO/nrn NM. If this occurs best chc of decent precip would stay mainly to the north and south of the area. Meanwhile, both models shows a stg cold front moving across the plains with gusty north winds behind it.

For Mon night into Tue, the ECMWF and GFS keep the two pieces of energy separated as the one piece over the nrn Rockies moves SSE across Colorado while the other piece of energy moves from nern NM into central Oklahoma. In addition, the GFS intensifies the upper level low as it moves into Oklahoma by late Mon night. The ECMWF has very little additional precip Mon night into Tue as much drier air spreads across the area. Meanwhile, the GFS has a band of precip over the ern plains Mon night but also decreases the chc of precip over the area on Tue. Winds will remain gusty over the plains Mon night into early Tue as well.
By Wed an upper level ridge will build over the area ahead of another possible system moving across on Thu. For now, Wed looks dry and warmer ahead of the next system.

CYS.name: Cheyenne
CYS.excerpt: A complex storm system will push across the western CONUS Sunday into early next week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Dry, warm, and breezy conditions are expected to continue through Thursday, with mild overnight lows.
- Chances for a few showers return Saturday (Halloween) with temperatures remaining mild.
- A pattern change to colder, wetter, and windier conditions is favored Sunday into Tuesday, but the details remain highly uncertain at this time.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Temperatures are going to be the hardest part of this short term forecast for tonight through Saturday morning. The models have indicated that a stratus deck will blanket the Nebraska Panhandle much like what has covered Sidney, Nebraska the entire day. This low stratus deck will insulate the surface, stabilizing the temperatures at some point through the night. Meanwhile most of Southeast Wyoming looks to be covered in high based clouds allowing for a little bit more cooling than what might occur in the Panhandle. So for the most part I have temperatures in the upper 30's for most of Southeast Wyoming and temperatures in the low to mid 40's for the Nebraska Panhandle area anticipating that low stratus deck to form. Patchy fog was also put into the grids as the stable atmosphere may lead to some fog production with visibility reductions as low as 1SM or possibly down to a quarter mile. High temperatures tomorrow look to be in the 50's and 60's but if the cloud layer behaves like it did over Sidney those temperatures may need to be dropped into the low 50's due to lack of diurnal heating. But no precipitation chances are expected in the short term forecast.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: The Long term forecast is pretty complex. Saturday morning a weak shortwave that's going to push through the western portion of Wyoming giving a chance for some morning to early afternoon showers for the southwestern corner of Carbon county. Everywhere else in the forecast area will see dry conditions and temperatures in the upper 50's to low 60's. Around trick or treating time most of the area will be hovering around 45 degrees for some possible light jacket conditions with the light winds.

A complex storm system will push across the western CONUS Sunday into early next week. Two major players will make up this system: first, a strong, moisture-laden upper level low riding the subtropical jet stream into the southwest and second, a potent Pacific trough pushing into the northwest. The primary questions concerning the evolution of this system are if, when, and where the two approaching systems might merge together. The model guidance has a hard time resolving this event often flip flopping how cold the air aloft will be and how much forcing will be present during the next few days. Latest probabilities are a 50 percent chance for 5 inches of snow concentrated on our mountain peaks and adjacent areas above 9,000t and possibly 1-3 inches for areas like Rawlins and Laramie as they sit at roughly 7,000ft. Then for areas for along and east of the I-25 corridor the 50 percent chance is for an inch or less as it may be too warm most of the time for adequate snow accumulation. The 90th percentile which would favor colder temperatures aloft and an earlier merger has about 10 inches for our peaks, 3-5 inches for Laramie and Rawlins and 1-2 inches of snow along the I-25 corridor with trace to an inch about as far east as Kimball Nebraska. Some of the major news networks have already begun posting the clickbait potential focusing on the very upper end of the accumulation amounts. But if the air aloft stays between 3-6C instead of diving into the negatives then we are more likely to end up with a decent amount of rain and very little snow Sunday through Tuesday. The 10 percentile encompasses this scenario a little better and the snow accumulation becomes 1-2 inches for our mountain tops and a trace amount for Laramie and Rawlins. For areas along and east of I-25 the precipitation would most likely stay as rain for majority of the time and have a rain/snow mix during the heavier rain portions. The high-resolution models take their first stab at the system soon and start to resolve the system and throw their weight towards the most likely scenario.

GJT.name: Grand Junction
GJT.excerpt: A cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 feet by Monday morning and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Precipitation chances return Friday PM with quick-hitting showers and storms for the lower elevations and flurries above 10,000 feet.
- Another round of 1 to 3 inches of rain for parts of southeast Utah and Southwest Colorado is possible Sunday into Monday.
- Flooding/flash flooding concerns increase Sunday into Monday, especially for areas that have saturated soils from last week's rain. A Flood Watch has been issued.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: ISOLATED TO SCATTERED SHOWERS FRIDAY AND SATURDAY:

A shortwave trough passes through the region Friday evening bringing a quick-hitting round of showers and storms to the region that will favor the higher terrain. Warm surface temperatures support rain being the primary precipitation type, with light snow possible above 10,000 feet. If thunderstorms develop, quick bursts of heavy rainfall could lead to isolated flooding issues, especially over areas still recovering from the last round of flooding.
WETTER AND UNSETTLED BY SUNDAY AND MONDAY:

A stronger surge of moisture an Atmospheric River (AR) arrives by Sunday. This AR will begin taking a southern track through Baja California, propagating through the Desert Southwest. There continues to be some uncertainty in the northern extent of the richer moisture, although confidence is high enough to introduce a Flood Watch for parts of southeast Utah and southwest Colorado that feature fatigued soils from recent rainfall and flooding. This is where there is the highest potential for 1 to 3 inches of rainfall Sunday into Monday. Please see the Hydrology section below for additional information on the potential for flooding and flash flooding with this system.

A cold front pushes through from northwest to southeast Sunday night into Monday, with snow levels dropping to around 8,000 feet by Monday morning and close to 7,000 ft by the evening as colder air pushes behind the front. Slippery stretches are likely over mountain passes. Keep an eye on the forecast if you plan to travel on Monday. Precipitation will taper off Monday evening, with cooler and drier conditions anticipated Tuesday and beyond.

PUB.name: Pueblo
PUB.excerpt: Tuesday through Thursday...the upper storm system is forecast to park itself across eastern Kansas for mid week.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - A few showers and possible thunderstorms due to passing waves are possible for the mountains Friday and Saturday.
- Very heavy rainfall for the San Juan Mountains will likely lead to another round of flooding, transitioning to snow over the mountains late in the event.
- A strong cold front will arrive on the Plains Monday, with winds in excess of 40 mph. Winds could prevail into Tuesday.

sections.name: Update
paragraphs: After coordination with surrounding offices, went ahead and issued a Dense Fog Advisory for portions of the plains late tonight through tomorrow morning. It is effect for Pueblo, Crowley, Otero, Kiowa, Bent and Prowers counties from 10 PM tonight through 10 AM tomorrow morning. Visibility is expected to drop down to less than 1/4 mile at times within the advisory area, and motorists are urged to allow extra travel time and stopping distance when driving in those areas.

sections.name: Short Term
paragraphs: Quiet weather is expected across the CWA today. Highs will be in the 50s and 60s, with the potential for some areas in the southern plains to reach 70. There is a chance for an isolated shower to reach into far SE CO tonight as some energy moves through the TX/OK panhandle, but weaker forcing and moisture will keep any precipitation very limited.

Fog returns to the eastern plains Friday morning as an unusually moist low-level airmass remains in place. Fog is expected to generally stay east of Pueblo County. Visibility will rapidly decrease in this area, falling to around 1-3 miles near the Kansas border. Remember to exercise caution when travailing. Fog will clear around 10am.

Friday afternoon will bring a slight chance of an isolated shower or thunderstorm to far SE CO. The main instability axis, moisture, and forcing are all displaced to our south, however the northern extent may clip part of our CWA. With MUCAPE of 500-1000 J/kg lingering, the possibility of a stray thunderstorm developing and crossing the SE CO border cannot be ruled out. Severe thresholds are not expected to be met.
Overnight Friday, a sfc trough will develop across eastern UT and western CO. This will act to bring the first wave of precipitation into the San Juans in association with the next system.

sections.name: Long Term
paragraphs: There is good agreement through much of the extended period, with a heavy rainfall event and very high elevation snowfall along the Continental Divide. Mountain flooding and windy conditions on the Plains are likely.

Saturday...a weak upper wave embedded in southwest flow will lead to showers and isolated thunderstorms along the Continental Divide by the afternoon. Lightning will be the main concern with any thunderstorms.

Saturday night through Monday...two upper waves are forecast to combine across southern Colorado during this period. The first, and upper wave moving in off the Baja Coast is forecast to lift northeast across the Desert Southwest, ahead of a secondary system out of the Pacific Northwest. The first upper wave will begin to impact the Continental Divide Saturday night into Sunday morning. PWAT values in excess of 0.8 to 1.1 inches will spread north across Colorado by Sunday morning. This will help promote heavy rainfall across the San Juan Range on Sunday. Snow levels will initially be high, above 12 kft, and the tropical nature help to produce heavy rainfall on Sunday. There could be a few lightning strikes embedded over the mountains. Flooding on area streams and rivers is likely across the San Juan Mountains, down into the San Luis Valley. This will be monitored closely.

Moving into Sunday night, the secondary wave will quickly fill in behind the initial wave. This will help lower snow levels to near 8500 feet by Monday morning. Precipitation will remain heavy across the San Juan Range. For elevations above 10 kft, snow probabilities increase, with 10 to 15 inches possible Sunday night into Monday. Lower elevations will continue to moderate to periods of heavy rainfall, and continued flooding potential.

Across the Plains, a cold front will arrive Monday morning, with very strong winds developing behind the northerly push. Model guidance in general agreement with showers developing along the Eastern Mountains, south along the Raton Mesa by late morning. This activity will continue south and east through the afternoon. At this time, around a quarter to half inch of rainfall is possible along the lee slopes and Raton Ridge before precipitation ends Monday evening. Snow levels on the eastern side will remain high, lower to near 9 kft by Monday afternoon. Snow amounts of a couple inches are possible up high.

East on the Plains, wind will be the main concern. Widespread strong northerly winds are forecast to prevail Monday afternoon and night. Gusts in excess of 40 mph will be possible, especially out near the Kansas border. There is some guidance indicating winds could be stronger, approaching 50 mph. We will continue to monitor wind conditions as the storm system approaches.

Temperatures look to remain warm both Sunday and Monday across the Plains. Highs in the 60s are forecast for Sunday, with around 5 to 10 degrees cooling behind the cold front on Monday, down into the 50s and lower 60s.

Tuesday through Thursday...the upper storm system is forecast to park itself across eastern Kansas for mid week. While precipitation come to an end Monday evening, the tight pressure gradient will keep winds gusting across the Plains Tuesday and Wednesday, before upper level ridging build across southern Colorado on Thursday. Temperatures will remain cool, with mostly 50s across the lower elevations. Winds with gusts 30 to 40 mph will remain possible on the Plains Tuesday and Wednesday, decreasing on Thursday.

SLC.name: Salt Lake City
SLC.excerpt: As the trough exits, strong high pressure is expected to move in beginning late Monday, though temperatures will stay on the cold side (up to 10F below seasonal normals) through midweek.

sections.name: Key Messages
paragraphs: - Tropical moisture will move into the region on Friday, leading to scattered showers and thunderstorms capable of producing heavy rainfall that could lead to flash flooding, particularly over southwest Utah.

- After a relative lull in precipitation on Saturday, a strong atmospheric river will interact with a strong cold front Sunday into Monday, resulting in widespread moderate to heavy precipitation across the region. This will increase the potential for flash flooding once again and bring accumulating snow to the mountains.
- Dry and unseasonably cool conditions are then expected through about midweek before a more active pattern returns.

sections.name: Discussion
paragraphs: Utah and southwest Wyoming is under an increasing southwest flow this evening ahead of a series of troughs along the Pacific coast. This has brought pockets of mid and high level cloudiness over the area and is starting to draw tropical moisture northward. Satellite derived PWs, which were predominately in the 0.2 to 0.3 inch range eight hours ago are now in the 0.3 to 0.5 inch range, with these values only expected to increase through Friday morning, particularly over southern Utah. The approach of the weakening southern trough will also provide some favorable instability, primarily focused over southwest Utah. Thus, anticipating the potential of scattered showers to develop over much of the area tomorrow afternoon, though chance of precip is much less over northern portions of the area. Southwest Utah is expected to be the focused, however, with the threat of heavy rain that could lead to flash flooding increasing for areas like lower Washington county and Zion National Park. Elsewhere, flash flooding is expected to be more isolated in nature.

This initial push of tropical moisture is expected to lift out of the area during the day Saturday, providing a relative lull in precipitation for much of the area, though at least some showers are expected to linger. Then attention turns to the stronger trough still expected to be parked off the Pacific coast. This system is expected to track across Utah and southwest Wyoming during the day Sunday into Monday morning, with the persistent southerly flow tapping into moisture from a potent atmospheric river. This combination of deep moisture and strong instability will result in widespread coverage of valley rain and mountain snow across the area, with the threat of flash flooding heightened, particularly over southern Utah. Flows remain high from other recent rain events, so flows remain high, increasing the threat. This will also bring accumulating snow to all of Utah's mountains. Snow levels will start on the high side, in the 8,000 to 9,000 foot range, but could drop as low as 6,500 feet by Monday morning with a good amount of cold air moving in. Will need to monitor for the potential for some significant snow accumulations in the northern mountains that could impact travel. The one limiting factor to the Sunday/Monday system is that guidance has been consistent in showing it to be quite progressive in nature, with most precipitation ending Monday morning.

As the trough exits, strong high pressure is expected to move in beginning late Monday, though temperatures will stay on the cold side (up to 10F below seasonal normals) through midweek. Long range guidance continues to show a lack of a blocking ridge off the Pacific coast which, as the ridge tracks east for the latter half of the week, will open up the region to additional storm systems through next weekend, which will likely result in another wetter than normal period.

2755.travel_advice: Watch for signs of unstable snow such as recent avalanches, cracking in the snow, and audible collapsing. Avoid traveling on or under similar slopes.

product.author: Ben Pritchett
bottom_line: An avalanche accident on the east side of Mt. Bross highlights that you can trigger a dangerous avalanche at the highest elevations (above about 12,500 feet) of the Central and Southern Mountains. West, north, and east-facing slopes hold multiple layers of snow from several storms in October. Deeper, wind-drifted slopes may be the most enticing for early-season snow travel, but they're also the slopes most likely to release an avalanche one to two feet deep.

Clouds build from the southwest on Friday ahead of a small initial wave of moisture. Friday night, expect light rain below around 10,000 feet, and up to six or eight inches of snow in the favored portions of the San Juan Mountains by Saturday morning, with less precipitation to the north. Saturday, the moisture tap dries out, before a stronger storm rolls in early Sunday.

On Sunday, a deep east-bound low-pressure trough brings initially warm conditions, with snow levels around 11,000 feet. Sunday night into early Monday, a cold front intensifies snowfall and pushes snow levels down to around 8,000 feet. By the end of the day Monday, expect storm totals of 1 to 2 feet of snow in the San Juan Mountains with half that amount through the Central and Northern Mountains.
Early-season travelers, including hunters and hikers, should use caution on steep terrain because even shallow snow on grassy slopes, rock slabs, or old snowfields can slide.

We will provide updates as needed until our daily forecasts resume on November 1, 2026. Please continue submitting your field observations, and check our website for real-time weather station data and model forecasts.

product.author: Kevin Studley
hazard_discussion: Avalanche Forecasting Operations Have Come to a Close for the 2026-26 Season
Have a safe spring in the mountains. Continue to remain vigilant and flexible while traveling in the mountains this spring.
OBSERVATIONS

Observations are still greatly appreciated. Spring-time observations are extremely helpful as forecast operations have come to a close. If you're out in the mountains, submit an observation to let the rest of the public know what's going on out there. Even a simple weather observation can be very useful.
• View recent observations HERE
• Submit an observation HERE
• Recent photos and videos HERE
Snow and Avalanche Information
• Dry Slab avalanche problems such as storm slab and wind slab avalanches are most likely during and immediately following a storm.

• Wet Loose avalanches are expected during warmups and (even brief) clear, sunny weather events, and rain events. Watch for pinwheels and rollerballs as an indicator the snow is becoming damp. If you're sinking into soft, mushy snow, it's time to turn around or find a different aspect.

• Wet Slab avalanches become likely during rain events and with multiple nights above freezing. Wet slabs occur when melt water pools and lubricates crusts or older persistent weak layers. Wet slab avalanches are notoriously difficult to predict.
• Cornices are large and often become unstable during prolonged warmups. Give yourself plenty of space above and below them. They tend to begin shedding during warming and/or rain events.
• Dry Loose Snow avalanches are expected during and immediately after a storm, particularly on shaded, north-facing slopes.

• Glide avalanches typically fail in similar spots year after year after an abundance of meltwater has saturated the ground or lower snowpack. Glide avalanches can occur in steep terrain, on smooth grassy slopes or on large slabs of rock. Look for glide cracks opening up during spring.
WEATHER
• Click HERE to view our Weather Station Map page with updated webcams
• Click HERE to view our Weather Tools page
• Spring weather patterns are often erratic and snow conditions can change quickly during spring weather. Be attentive to these changes and remain flexible with your travel plans.
• Rain on snow events can create dangerous avalanche conditions in a short period of time.
• Spring time means a higher sun angle, with direct solar radiation on the snowpack. Even a brief dose of sunshine can quickly alter the snow surface.

• Overcast skies and snow showers can open up to full sunshine in a matter of minutes. Convective snow showers can be spotty and difficult to forecast. Temperatures can vary depending on elevation and unexpected cloud cover can significantly alter a weather forecast.
OTHER CONSIDERATIONS
• Travel
• As people push into steeper, more consequential terrain, remember to maintain safe travel protocols and not let your guard down just because it's sunny and warm.
• During melt-freeze cycles, pay attention to "slide-for-life" circumstances, particularly during morning travel.
• Be mindful of terrain selection and timing. Identify terrain traps and be prepared to avoid/manage them.
• Spring Mindset

• Springtime is when mountain travelers push for bigger objectives. We have greater confidence in the stability of the snowpack and the high sun angle makes us feel ready to charge. As we start stepping out into bigger terrain in the mountains, be mindful of consequences (ask yourself, "If this slides, what will happen?"). Choose your terrain appropriately and manage new/surface snow problems accordingly. Be aware that dynamic weather can have quick impacts on the snow surface. A common theme I've noticed over the last 15 years playing in steep, snowy mountains is that experienced, seasoned people often get caught in small avalanches in big terrain during the spring. We have a tendency to underestimate "manageable" new snow problems like wind slab and loose snow. Pay attention to changing weather and know that small shifts in spring weather can have dramatic impacts on the upper snowpack.

(Precipitation data are recorded from Secesh SNOTEL site at 6540')
